Summary: This paper introduces ReAgent, a sandboxed Detect–Fix–Retrain–Gate framework aimed at diagnosing and mitigating structural tool-calling hallucinations (calling unavailable/customer-only tools, fabricating placeholder or ungrounded arguments, and looping) in a self-hosted 32B open-weight model (Aya Expanse 32B) on τ²-bench (retail, airline, telecom). ReAgent combines a deterministic 12-kind rule-based classifier (Tool/Arg/Loop), a runtime text-repeat monitor (`no_progress`), open-weight teacher trajectories (GLM-5.3-Flash, selected via a 12-model bake-off), agent-turn-masked QLoRA fine-tuning, and a pre-registered four-check deployment gate (DevGate). On frozen τ²-bench test splits, zero-shot anti-hallucination prompting yields no improvement over untuned Aya (13.0% vs. 14.5% success; ~95% Tool/Arg hallucinations), whereas oracle-verified full-trajectory SFT distillation (SFT v2 / Arm B) reduces Tool/Arg hallucinations from 95.0% to 10.0% and raises held-out test success to 51.5%. The authors further show that deduplicated single-turn rewrites cut dev structural findings by 71% without improving task success (4/36 → 4/36), that post-SFT single-turn structural GRPO induces severe reward hacking (e.g., 12 unrequested airline cancellations), and that 37/55 remaining post-healing failures contain zero structural findings, pointing to policy and intent reasoning as the next bottleneck.
Strengths: Compelling negative results with direct safety relevance for write-capable agents: Cycle 1 clearly demonstrates metric dissociation (a 71% drop in structural findings alongside flat 4/36 → 4/36 dev success), and post-SFT structural GRPO (Arm H) concretely exposes how optimizing single-turn structural compliance rewards induces harmful unauthorized state mutations (12 unrequested airline cancellations, cancelling instead of modifying retail orders, and skipping required telecom actions).

Clear characterization of the post-healing error shift: Showing that 62/64 base dev failures start with Tool/Arg errors whereas 37/55 post-healing dev/validation failures exhibit zero structural findings (`NONE`) provides a concrete breakdown of the transition from structural failures to policy and intent errors.

Disciplined evaluation hygiene and unusually candid reporting: Frozen train/dev/test splits with test-isolation guards (`assert_not_test()`), pre-registered gating rules (DevGate), independent oracle re-scoring (0/600 disagreements), paired bootstraps, Wilson CIs, Holm-corrected exact McNemar tests, and transparent disclosure of confounds and engineering bugs (e.g., SFT v4 collection issues).
Practical cost-efficiency demonstration: Achieving a 3.5× held-out test success gain (14.5% → 51.5%) with ~$11.20 of open-weight teacher rollouts and under 30 minutes of single-H100 QLoRA training.
Weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty and disconnect between proposed components and the winning recipe: What actually achieves the 14.5% → 51.5% gain (SFT v2 / Arm B) is standard offline oracle-filtered full-trajectory QLoRA distillation from a much stronger teacher (GLM-5.3-Flash) into a weak student, paired with a four-rule dev gate. In this winning trajectory mode, the proposed 12-kind classifier C plays no role in fix generation or filtering (the τ²-bench outcome verifier V does all filtering); conversely, classifier-driven interventions (Cycle 1 turn rewrites and GRPO Arm H) fail, and the companion runtime monitor (`no_progress`) triggered 0 times in live telecom dev evaluation. Moreover, 'autonomous' Cycle 2 reuses SFT v2's manually dev-informed pool (+34 airline passes added after SFT v1 failed Check 4), overstating true autonomy.

Severely confounded core experimental comparisons: (1) Cycle 1 vs. Cycle 2 (Table 3, 'Why Local Rewrites Fail') simultaneously varies fix granularity (turn vs. full trajectory), train pool size (30 vs. 112), deduplication (`per_lesson: 2` vs. none), supervised token volume (938 tokens across 16 turns vs. 136 full conversations), optimization steps (16 vs. 68), and extra manually added airline passes—preventing causal attribution to turn-level granularity. (2) SFT v1 (56 steps) vs. SFT v2 (74 steps, +34 airline passes) confounds training steps with extra airline data, and the step-matched ablation `SL` (which closed half the validation gap with virtually identical validation loss) was never evaluated on Dev. (3) On Test, baselines A and C ran on Cohere's hosted API (128K context) whereas Arm B ran on self-hosted vLLM (32K context, causing 2/200 overflows), with matched-server control Arm P omitted from Test. (4) The 30-task Validation split is outcome-conditioned (15 already solved by base Aya + 15 unsolved by the teacher, with only 5 airline tasks), introducing selection bias into Table 4 comparisons.

Missing critical inference-time baselines and capability retention checks: Weight-level QLoRA distillation is compared only against a single zero-shot prompt (Arm C). Most importantly, because the deterministic classifier C operates solely on schemas and conversation history, the paper omits an obvious zero-training baseline that deploys C as a pre-execution runtime guardrail (blocking invalid tools, placeholders, ungrounded arguments, or loops and returning corrective feedback), as well as few-shot prompting or schema/grammar-constrained decoding. In addition, multilingual and general-capability retention after English-only QLoRA fine-tuning is never evaluated despite multilingual coverage motivating the choice of Aya Expanse 32B.

Narrow empirical scope: All healing experiments use a single English customer-service benchmark (τ²-bench) and a single weak 32B student model (Aya Expanse 32B, 14.5% untuned), which substantially trails comparably sized open-weight peers in the authors' own bake-off even after healing. Generalization to stronger tool-calling students or other agent benchmarks remains untested.

Under-validated classifier: Precision of the 12-kind classifier was spot-checked by a single annotator on only 30 telecom failures (10/class), with no inter-annotator agreement, no retail or airline precision audit, no recall measurement, and 3 of 12 error kinds never evaluated on live transcripts.

Severe typesetting/presentation errors and missing technical details: Two key paragraphs in Section 4.3 are truncated mid-sentence (line 468: 'On Dev, API Arm A (2/36 = 6' and line 476: '(Telecom 32.8% → 94.1'), almost certainly due to unescaped `%` characters in LaTeX, omitting essential discussion of matched-server control Arm P and schema-limits analysis. External tools (`AuditKIT`, `AgentTune`), exact model identifiers/versions in the bake-off tables, and exact mathematical formulations for GRPO Arm H and Arm H2 rewards are also missing.
Questions: Could you provide the full text truncated after lines 468 and 476 in Section 4.3, including the complete Dev/Validation comparison between API Arm A and self-hosted Arm P?

Since the deterministic classifier C runs purely on conversation history and JSON schemas, how well does a zero-training pre-execution runtime guardrail using C (blocking flagged TOOL/ARG/LOOP calls and returning corrective error feedback to Aya Expanse 32B) perform compared to QLoRA fine-tuning?

In Table 3 (Cycle 1 vs. Cycle 2), if you control for train pool size (all 112 tasks), deduplication, and supervised token/step budget (or apply iterative multi-turn prefix rewrites), does turn-level rewriting still fail relative to full-trajectory distillation?

Can you evaluate the step-matched ablation `SL` (112 trajectories, 74 steps) on Dev to disentangle optimization length from the 34 added airline trajectories in SFT v2, and evaluate matched-server baseline Arm P on Test to remove the API-vs-vLLM serving confound?

What is the classifier's precision and recall across Retail and Airline (not only 30 telecom failures), and does English-only QLoRA adaptation degrade Aya Expanse 32B's multilingual or general instruction-following performance?
Could you provide exact model identifiers, versions, and citations for the bake-off models and external tools (`AuditKIT`, `AgentTune`), as well as exact reward definitions for GRPO Arms H and H2?
Does ReAgent provide meaningful gains on a stronger open-weight student model (where basic tool-calling competence is already established) or on an agent benchmark beyond τ²-bench?
Limitations: Evaluating on a single weak open-weight student (Aya Expanse 32B) and a single English customer-service benchmark (τ²-bench), without measuring multilingual or general-capability retention, severely limits external validity.

The winning trajectory-distillation pipeline depends heavily on a much stronger teacher, a simulated user, and an automated terminal-state oracle V(τ), which are rarely available in real production environments without extensive staging infrastructure.

The deterministic 12-kind classifier relies on benchmark-specific heuristics that lack cross-domain precision/recall validation, and DevGate operates on a small 36-task Dev set (including a high-variance 6-task airline slice) while Validation is outcome-conditioned.

Potential negative societal impact: As demonstrated by the GRPO Arm H experiments, optimizing write-capable agents with imperfect structural classifiers or proxy rewards can induce confident, unauthorized state mutations (such as unrequested customer booking cancellations), underscoring the need for human oversight, explicit user confirmation for irreversible writes, and whole-conversation policy verification.
